# Configuration File

Rex configuration is written in [Lua](https://www.lua.org) and lives in
a single file: `init.lua`. It binds keys, defines custom actions, declares
the other servers you connect to, and more. It can load other Lua files
(via `require`) so you can split your configuration up as you'd like.

Rex doesn't require any configuration, so start using Rex without it
and start a configuration file when there is something you want to change.

## File Location

On **macOS and Linux**, the file is at `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/rex/init.lua` when
that environment variable is set and `~/.config/rex/init.lua` when it isn't.

On **Windows**, the file is at `%AppData%\rex\init.lua`.

Set `REX_CONFIG` to the path of another file to use that one instead.
This environment variable must be set in the environment of the Rex server
process, since the server is what reads the file.

## Quick Example

Here is a minimal configuration example with one keybinding:

```lua
rex.bind("cmd+d", "pane.split", { direction = "right" })
```

Reload the configuration with the CLI. Connected clients will be notified of
the new configuration and it will take effect immediately. Rex does not
currently watch for file changes; you must use the CLI.

```sh
rex config reload
```

The configuration file is read by the Rex server, so it lives on the same
machine as the server. `rex config reload` must also be run on that machine;
it is refused over a remote connection.

Press <kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>D</kbd> and the focused pane splits to the right.

The [Lua API reference](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/reference/lua.md) lists all available Lua APIs.

## Validation

`rex config check` loads the file without changing anything and reports any
issues. If there are no issues, it reports the changes it found:

```
$ rex config check
path: /Users/you/.config/rex/init.lua
exists: yes
bindings: 8
removals: 0
modes: 1
actions: 0
```

Both commands print the file's mistakes and exit with status 1 if any of them
is an error. Give `rex config check` a path to check a file other than your
own, such as a draft.

### Validation Errors

A bad call to a `rex` function is skipped, and the rest of the file still
loads. Here line 2 passes a table where a key belongs:

```lua
rex.bind("cmd+d", "pane.split", { direction = "right" })
rex.bind({ "cmd+k" }, "pane.split")
rex.bind("ctrl+b>c", "window.new")
```

```
$ rex config check
...
bindings: 2
...
error init.lua:2: rex.bind: expected a string, got table
Error: the configuration has errors
```

The other two bindings still work.

A mistake Lua itself can't get past, such as a syntax error, fails the whole
load. When that happens on a reload, the server keeps the bindings and actions
from the last load that worked.

Some mistakes can't be seen from the file alone. Whether `pane.split` is a
real action depends on the client, because clients provide those actions.
`rex keymap` asks the running server for the merged result and reports these.

## Splitting Configuration

`require` loads other Lua files stored beside it:

```lua
-- ~/.config/rex/init.lua
require("keys")
```

```lua
-- ~/.config/rex/keys.lua
rex.bind("cmd+d", "pane.split", { direction = "right" })
rex.bind("ctrl+b>c", "window.new")
```

Mistakes are reported with the name of the file they are in, such as
`keys.lua:2`.

## Execution Model

The file runs from top to bottom each time it loads.

This load-time execution is for defining bindings, actions, etc. The callbacks
for these are deferred until they're invoked. Rex APIs such as listing sessions
or creating a new window do not work at load-time, since API calls are made on
behalf of a client and load-time has no client. They're reported as a warning
and the rest of the file still loads.

Example:

```lua
rex.action{
  name  = "scratch",
  title = "Open Scratch Window",
  run   = function(ctx, args)
    rex.session.new_window{
      layout = rex.layout.block{
        flavor = "com.superlogical.terminal.shell",
      },
    }
  end,
}
```

This defines the `scratch` action, but it doesn't invoke the callback
with `rex.session.new_window` until the action is actually invoked via
the command palette, a keybinding, etc.

To run Lua once from top to bottom against a live session, write a separate
script and run it with `rex do` instead.

# Key Sequences

A key sequence is two or more keys pressed one after another, such as
<kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>B</kbd> and then <kbd>C</kbd>. Sequences are bound with
`rex.bind` like any other [keyboard shortcut](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/customize/keyboard-shortcuts.md),
with the keys joined by `>`:

```lua
rex.bind("ctrl+b>c", "client.tab.new")
rex.bind("ctrl+b>z", "pane.zoom")
```

Each key in a sequence is written the same way as a single key, modifiers
included. A sequence can be longer than two keys:

```lua
rex.bind("ctrl+b>shift+5", "pane.split", { direction = "right" })
rex.bind("ctrl+x>ctrl+k>s", "session.switch")
```

Press <kbd>Escape</kbd> partway through a sequence to cancel it.

## Example: Tmux Bindings

```lua
rex.bind("ctrl+b>c", "client.tab.new")
rex.bind("ctrl+b>n", "client.tab.next")
rex.bind("ctrl+b>p", "client.tab.previous")
-- % and " on a US layout
rex.bind("ctrl+b>shift+5", "pane.split", { direction = "right" })
rex.bind("ctrl+b>shift+'", "pane.split", { direction = "down" })
rex.bind("ctrl+b>z", "pane.zoom")
rex.bind("ctrl+b>x", "pane.close")

-- Press Ctrl+B twice to send one to the terminal
rex.bind("ctrl+b>ctrl+b", "pane.send_key", { key = "ctrl+b" })
```

Note the last binding. Once <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>B</kbd> starts a sequence
it no longer reaches the terminal by itself, so programs that use it need
another way to receive it.

## Binding vs. Sequence Conflict

A key either runs an action immediately or starts a sequence. It can't do
both, because Rex would have to wait to find out which you meant.

When a key is bound both ways, the newer binding wins and the older one never
runs:

```lua
rex.bind("cmd+k", "pane.zoom")         -- never runs
rex.bind("cmd+k>s", "session.switch")  -- cmd+k starts a sequence
```

With the two lines swapped, <kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>K</kbd> zooms immediately and
the sequence can never start.

The same rule applies across the [three places shortcuts come from](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/customize/keyboard-shortcuts.md#how-shortcuts-are-resolved).
A sequence in your configuration file hides the client's default shortcut for
its first key, and a shortcut set in the app hides a sequence in the file that
starts with the same key.

Rex doesn't reorder anything to avoid this. Instead, the client is given a
warning that names both bindings and where each was written.

## Removing a Sequence

`rex.unbind` removes exactly one binding:

```lua
rex.unbind("ctrl+b>c")   -- removes this one sequence
rex.unbind("ctrl+b")     -- removes ctrl+b alone, and no sequences
```

Unbinding a key never removes the sequences that start with it. Each sequence
has to be unbound by its full name. A future change to Rex will allow
removing all sequences by prefix.

## Binding a Lua Function

A sequence can run a Lua function. The function is called when the last key of
the sequence is pressed:

```lua
rex.bind("ctrl+x>ctrl+s", function(ctx, ev)
  -- ev.prefix is { "ctrl+x" } and ev.keybinding is "ctrl+s"
  return true
end)
```

`ev.keybinding` is the last key and `ev.prefix` is a list of the keys before
it. One function bound to several sequences can use these to tell which one
was pressed. A function bound to a single key has no `ev.prefix`.

If the function returns `false` or nothing, only the last key is sent to the
focused terminal. The earlier keys were already consumed by the client.

# Key Modes

A key mode is a named set of [keyboard shortcuts](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/customize/keyboard-shortcuts.md)
that only apply while the mode is active. Modes let ordinary keys do something
else for a while, such as making the arrow keys resize panes. They are also
called "key tables" in other software.

```lua
rex.bind("cmd+r", "client.mode.enter", { name = "resize" })

rex.bind("resize/left", "pane.resize", { direction = "left" })
rex.bind("resize/right", "pane.resize", { direction = "right" })
rex.bind("resize/up", "pane.resize", { direction = "up" })
rex.bind("resize/down", "pane.resize", { direction = "down" })
```

Press <kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>R</kbd> to enter the mode. The arrow keys now resize
the focused pane. Press <kbd>Escape</kbd> to leave the mode, and the arrow
keys go back to what they did before.

## Binding a Key in a Mode

To bind a key in a mode, write the mode's name and a slash `/` before the key:

```lua
rex.bind("resize/shift+left", "pane.resize", {
  direction = "left",
  amount = 15,
})
```

A mode exists as soon as a key is bound in it. A mode name may contain only
lowercase letters, digits, underscores, and hyphens.

The key after the slash can be anything a shortcut outside a mode can be,
including a [key sequence](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/customize/key-sequences.md) such as `resize/g>g`.

Bindings in a mode are separate from bindings outside it. Binding `resize/left`
doesn't change what <kbd>Left</kbd> does outside the mode.

A binding in a mode must name an action. To run Lua from a mode, define a
[custom action](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/customize/actions.md) and bind that.

## Entering and Leaving a Mode

The client provides three actions for moving between modes. Bind them like any
other action:

| Action | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `client.mode.enter` | Enters the mode given by `name`. |
| `client.mode.exit` | Leaves the current mode. |
| `client.mode.exit_all` | Leaves every mode. |

<kbd>Escape</kbd> also leaves the current mode, unless the mode binds
<kbd>Escape</kbd> to something else.

A mode stays active until you leave it. To leave automatically after one
shortcut, enter it with `once`:

```lua
rex.bind("cmd+r", "client.mode.enter", {
  name = "resize",
  once = true,
})
```

Modes can be entered from inside other modes. The most recently entered mode
is checked first, and `client.mode.exit` leaves only that one.

## Unbound Keys in a Mode

By default, a key the mode doesn't bind does what it does outside the mode.
In the resize example, you can still type in the terminal while the mode is
active.

Declare the mode as `exclusive` to ignore those keys instead:

```lua
rex.mode("resize", { exclusive = true })
```

While an exclusive mode is active, only its own bindings do anything. This
avoids typing into a terminal by accident while you think you're resizing.

`rex.mode` is only needed to set options. `exclusive` is the only option.

## Removing Bindings

`rex.unbind` with a mode and a key removes that key's bindings in the mode
and **blocks** the key there. A blocked key does nothing while the mode is
active, even if it is bound outside the mode:

```lua
rex.unbind("resize/left")
```

Pass an action name to remove one binding without blocking the key:

```lua
rex.unbind("resize/left", "pane.resize")
```

To remove a whole mode, including its bindings, blocked keys, and options,
pass a table:

```lua
rex.unbind{ mode = "resize" }
```

`rex.unbind("left")` never touches a mode, and `rex.unbind("resize/left")`
never touches <kbd>Left</kbd> outside the mode.

## Example: Resize Mode

A complete resize mode, entered with <kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>R</kbd>:

```lua
rex.mode("resize", { exclusive = true })
rex.bind("cmd+r", "client.mode.enter", { name = "resize" })

rex.bind("resize/left", "pane.resize", { direction = "left" })
rex.bind("resize/right", "pane.resize", { direction = "right" })
rex.bind("resize/up", "pane.resize", { direction = "up" })
rex.bind("resize/down", "pane.resize", { direction = "down" })

-- Hold shift for bigger steps
rex.bind("resize/shift+left", "pane.resize", {
  direction = "left",
  amount = 15,
})
rex.bind("resize/shift+right", "pane.resize", {
  direction = "right",
  amount = 15,
})

rex.bind("resize/=", "pane.balance")
rex.bind("resize/enter", "client.mode.exit")
```

## Debugging

`rex keymap` lists every mode the server loaded after its bindings, along
with whether it is exclusive and which keys it blocks:

```
$ rex keymap
KEY           ACTION       ARGS                  SOURCE
resize/left   pane.resize  {"direction":"left"}  init.lua:4
...

MODE    EXCLUSIVE  BLOCKED
resize  yes        -
```

# Keyboard Shortcuts

Keyboard shortcuts are defined in the [configuration file](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/customize/config.md)
with `rex.bind` and removed with `rex.unbind`. A shortcut binds a key to an
**action**, such as splitting a pane or switching sessions.

```lua
rex.bind("cmd+e", "pane.zoom")
rex.bind("shift+cmd+d", "pane.split", { direction = "down" })
```

Run `rex config reload` after changing the file for the shortcuts to take
effect.

## Binding a Key

`rex.bind` takes a key, the name of an action, and optionally a table of
arguments for that action:

```lua
rex.bind(key, action, args)
```

Some actions require arguments and some have optional arguments. For
example, `pane.resize` requires a `direction` and accepts an optional
`amount`:

```lua
rex.bind("ctrl+alt+left", "pane.resize", { direction = "left" })
rex.bind("ctrl+alt+shift+left", "pane.resize", {
  direction = "left",
  amount = 15,
})
```

Binding a key that already has a binding replaces it. The newest binding
for a key always wins.

## Finding Actions

Actions are provided by the client, so the list depends on which client you
use. List the actions of a connected client with the CLI:

```
$ rex client ls
LABEL     CLIENT                KIND  PRINCIPAL          AGE     ID
my-mac    Rex Beta 0.1.0 (996)  app   uid 501 over unix  1h ago  db494d

$ rex -C my-mac actions
NAME                   TITLE             ARGS
client.tab.new         New Tab
client.tab.goto        Go to Tab         index
pane.split             Split Pane        direction
pane.zoom              Zoom Pane
pane.resize            Resize Pane       direction, amount?
pane.send_key          Send Key          key
session.switch         Change Session…
...
```

The `ARGS` column lists the arguments each action takes. An argument followed
by `?` is optional.

You can also define your own actions in Lua and bind keys to them. See
[Custom Actions](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/customize/actions.md).

## Writing Keys

A key is written as zero or more modifiers followed by one key, joined by
`+`. Case and the order of modifiers don't matter, so `shift+cmd+d` and
`Cmd+Shift+D` are the same key.

| Modifier | Also Written |
| --- | --- |
| `cmd` | `command`, `super`, `meta`, `win` |
| `ctrl` | `control` |
| `alt` | `opt`, `option` |
| `shift` | |

The key is a character such as `d`, `1`, or `,` or a name such as `enter`,
`escape`, `tab`, `space`, `backspace`, `delete`, `left`, `right`, `up`, `down`,
`home`, `end`, `pageup`, `pagedown`, or `f1` through `f12`.

Keys follow your keyboard layout: `ctrl+a` is whichever key types "a". To bind
a physical key regardless of layout, write its US-layout name in brackets,
such as `ctrl+[KeyA]`. The names are the
[W3C `KeyboardEvent.code` values](https://www.w3.org/TR/uievents-code/#code-value-tables),
such as `[Digit1]`, `[Slash]`, and `[ArrowLeft]`.

Write the key without shift applied. On a US layout, plus is `cmd+shift+=`,
not `cmd++`. Bindings are always matched on unshifted keys.

A shortcut can also be several keys pressed one after another, such as
`ctrl+b>c`. See [Key Sequences](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/customize/key-sequences.md).

Shortcuts can also be grouped into a mode that is only active when you enter
it, such as a mode for resizing panes. See [Key Modes](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/customize/key-modes.md).

## Removing a Shortcut

`rex.unbind` removes every binding for a key. It can be used to remove
a binding you set as well as unbind a key that the client defaults with:

```lua
rex.unbind("cmd+d")
```

Pass an action name to remove the key only when it is bound to that action:

```lua
rex.unbind("cmd+t", "client.tab.new")
```

An unbound key isn't handled by Rex at all, so it is sent to the focused
terminal.

To change what a default shortcut does, bind it. There is no need to unbind
it first:

```lua
-- Cmd+K clears the screen instead
rex.bind("cmd+k", "pane.send_key", { key = "ctrl+l" })
```

## How Shortcuts Are Resolved

A key can get its meaning from three places. From lowest to highest priority:

1. The default shortcuts the client ships with.
2. Your configuration file.
3. Shortcuts you set in the client itself, such as with the app's
   **Change Shortcut...** command.

A shortcut set in the app therefore wins over the configuration file. If a
binding in your file appears to do nothing, check that the app doesn't have its
own shortcut for the same key.

## Binding a Lua Function

A key can run a Lua function instead of an action. Return `true` to say the
key was handled:

```lua
rex.bind("ctrl+shift+n", function(ctx, ev)
  rex.session.new_window{
    layout = rex.layout.block{
      flavor = "com.superlogical.terminal.shell",
    },
  }
  return true
end)
```

The function can call any Rex API, such as `rex.session.new_window` above.
The [Lua API reference](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/reference/lua.md) has the full list.

If the function returns `false` or nothing, Rex tries the next-newest function
bound to the same key, and sends the key to the focused terminal if none of
them handle it.

A function binding has no name, so it doesn't appear in the command palette
and can't be run from the CLI. For anything you'd want to do more than one
way, define a [custom action](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/customize/actions.md) and bind the key to that.

## Inspecting Bindings

A configuration that loads other files with `require` can look at what they
bound and remove what it doesn't want. `rex.bindings()` returns every binding
made so far, in the order they were made.

```lua
require("keys")

-- Remove every sequence keys.lua bound behind ctrl+b
for _, b in ipairs(rex.bindings()) do
  if b.key:find("ctrl+b>", 1, true) == 1 then
    rex.unbind(b)
  end
end
```

Each binding is a table with `key`, `mode`, `action`, `args`, and `source`
(the file and line that made it). Passing one to `rex.unbind` removes exactly
that binding.

`rex.bindings` also accepts a filter on `key`, `mode`, or `action`, such as
`rex.bindings{ action = "pane.split" }`. `rex.modes()` does the same for
[key modes](https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/customize/key-modes.md).

These functions only see your configuration file and the files it loads. They
can't see the client's default shortcuts or the ones set in the app.

## Debugging

`rex config check` reports mistakes in the file itself, such as a key that
can't be parsed:

cmd+e        pane.zoom       -                     init.lua:1
...

local function run_command(argv, options)
  local result, err = rex.exec(argv, options)
  if err ~= nil then error(err, 0) end
  if not result.ok then error(result.stderr, 0) end
  return result.stdout

local function current_directory(ctx)
  if not ctx.block_id then return nil end
  -- Rex fills in the action's block ID. Shell integration reports a file URL.
  local result, err = rex.block.call("com.superlogical.terminal", "pwd", {})
  if err ~= nil then error(err, 0) end
  local pwd = result.pwd
  -- Before the shell reports its directory, use Rex's default directory.
  if pwd == nil or pwd == "" then return nil end
  if pwd:sub(1, 1) == "/" then return pwd end
  local path = pwd:match("^file://[^/]*(/.*)$")
  if not path then error("Terminal reported an unsupported directory: " .. pwd, 0) end
  return (path:gsub("%%(%x%x)", function(hex)
    return string.char(tonumber(hex, 16))
  end))
end

local function fish_layout(ctx, fish_command)

    flavor = "com.superlogical.terminal.shell",
    options = {

      shell = "none",

可以。Rex 原生支持两种做法，都不需要插件；区别在于“按键序列”与“真正的 prefix 模式”。

## 方案 A：键序列（最像 tmux 的按键习惯）

Rex 用 `>` 表示连续按键，官方文档本身就给了 tmux 示例：

```lua
-- ~/.config/rex/init.lua
rex.bind("ctrl+b>c", "client.tab.new")
rex.bind("ctrl+b>n", "client.tab.next")
rex.bind("ctrl+b>p", "client.tab.previous")

-- % 和 "（US 布局）
rex.bind("ctrl+b>shift+5", "pane.split", { direction = "right" })
rex.bind("ctrl+b>shift+'", "pane.split", { direction = "down" })

rex.bind("ctrl+b>z", "pane.zoom")
rex.bind("ctrl+b>x", "pane.close")

-- 连按两次前缀，向终端发送一个字面的 Ctrl+B
rex.bind("ctrl+b>ctrl+b", "pane.send_key", { key = "ctrl+b" })
```

- 按 `Ctrl+B` 后再按 `c`，就是 tmux 的手感。
- 序列中途按 `Escape` 取消。
- 每条命令仍是一条独立绑定，不是持久化的“prefix 状态”。

文档：<https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/customize/key-sequences>

## 方案 B：Key Mode（真正的 prefix 状态）

如果想让“按一下前缀，再按任意命令键”成为有状态的模式，用 key mode：

```lua
rex.bind("ctrl+b", "client.mode.enter", { name = "tmux", once = true })

rex.bind("tmux/c", "client.tab.new")
rex.bind("tmux/n", "client.tab.next")
rex.bind("tmux/p", "client.tab.previous")
rex.bind("tmux/z", "pane.zoom")
rex.bind("tmux/x", "pane.close")

-- 前缀按两次：发送字面 Ctrl+B
rex.bind("tmux/ctrl+b", "pane.send_key", { key = "ctrl+b" })
```

- `once = true`：执行完一个命令后自动退出该模式，最接近 tmux。
- 想更严格，可以加 `rex.mode("tmux", { exclusive = true })`，让模式内未绑定的键不落到终端；但这样按错键后要用 `Escape` 退出，和 tmux 的“未知命令直接取消”略有差异。
- 文档：<https://www.superlogical.com/rex/docs/customize/key-modes>

## 关键限制

1. **同一个键不能既单独执行动作、又开始序列。** 比如不能同时写 `rex.bind("ctrl+b", "client.mode.enter", ...)` 和 `rex.bind("ctrl+b>c", ...)`；后写的会赢，前者永远不触发。所以方案 A 和 B 要二选一，或者给它们用不同前缀键。
2. **优先级是：Rex 客户端里设置的快捷键 > `init.lua` > 客户端默认快捷键。** 如果 app 里已经给 `Ctrl+B` 设了快捷键，配置会被压住。可用 `rex keymap` 检查实际生效的绑定。
3. 前缀键被 Rex 消费后不会再传给终端；用 `ctrl+b>ctrl+b` 或 `tmux/ctrl+b` 补回字面按键。
4. 你现在仓库里的 `home/.config/rex/init.lua` 明确写着“no prefix key or key modes”，并且 `tests/validate/rex.lua` 断言所有绑定都不含 `>`、`/`，也没有 mode。如果改成前缀方案，这两处要一起更新。
5. 你现有配置特意保留了 `Ctrl+A` 和 `Ctrl+W` 给 shell；如果选前缀，建议继续用 `Ctrl+B` 或 `Ctrl+Space`，不要占用这两个。

```sh
rex config check ~/.config/rex/init.lua
rex config reload
rex keymap
```
